body: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic in Kandy, Sri Lanka, is one of the most important Buddhist sites in the world. While several locations claim to house relics of the Buddha, this specific temple is widely recognized for enshrining his left upper canine tooth. The teachings of the Buddha were transmitted by word of mouth passing his canine tooth. The relic holds immense spiritual and political significance; historically, it was believed that whoever possessed the tooth had the right to govern the country. The temple attracts thousands of pilgrims and tourists daily. Its importance to Buddhists is often likened to that of Mecca or the Vatican. During major festivals like the Esala Perahera, when the relic's casket is brought out in a grand procession, the streets become densely packed with devotees and impassable for blocks.

body: The Temple of the Tooth as a building is of secondary importance. Only its purpose, the storage and protection of the Dalada, the tooth of Buddha, is important. The veneration of the tooth is based on the belief that the spiritual power of the Buddha is stored in it. According to this, the tooth has the ability to act as a rainmaker, similar to the Bodhi tree during Buddha's enlightenment. This belief turned the religious relic into an instrument of political power. It passed through the hands of many Indian kings. The respective protector of the tooth was respected because he had religious support and his country could never be ravaged by drought. In Sri Lanka, the tooth was kept in the respective capital of the country. It was a kind of legitimation for the Sinhalese throne. Buddhists from all over the world come to Kandy to visit the Temple of the Tooth. The climax of this veneration is the annual Esala Perahera. body: emple of the Sacred Tooth Relic – A Revered Spiritual LandmarkLocated in the historic city of Kandy, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa) is one of Sri Lanka’s most significant religious and cultural landmarks. Known as the home of the Sacred Tooth Relic of the Buddha, this UNESCO World Heritage site attracts millions of visitors from around the world, offering a deeply spiritual and historically enriching experience.Historical & Religious SignificanceThe Tooth Relic is believed to have been in the possession of Buddha himself, making it one of the most sacred relics in the Buddhist world.The temple has been a center of religious and political significance throughout Sri Lanka’s history, with kings once holding the relic as a symbol of their right to rule.The intricate architecture, combining traditional Sinhalese and Buddhist designs, reflects the temple’s sacred status.What to Expect During Your VisitSacred Tooth Relic Shrine – The main attraction, where the relic is enshrined in a beautifully adorned chamber, is surrounded by a sense of reverence and peace.Drummers’ and Dancers’ Performances – Visitors can witness the traditional Perahera dances and drumming ceremonies during special occasions like the Esala Perahera festival, which takes place annually.Historical Artifacts & Exhibits – The temple also houses an exhibition of royal artifacts, paintings, and manuscripts, offering a glimpse into the history of Buddhism and Sri Lanka’s royal past.Serene Atmosphere – The temple’s surroundings, with its lush gardens and tranquil lake views, create a peaceful and contemplative environment for visitors.Why Visit the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic?✔ A deeply spiritual and historical experience✔ Architectural beauty with a rich Buddhist heritage✔ Home to one of Buddhism’s most revered relics✔ Stunning rituals and cultural performances, especially during festivals✔ Located in the scenic city of Kandy, a UNESCO World Heritage SiteVisiting the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic offers not only a deep dive into Sri Lanka’s rich spiritual heritage but also a chance to experience the serenity and cultural grandeur of this sacred site. It’s a must-visit for anyone traveling to Kandy or interested in Buddhism and Sri Lankan history

body: On the lake, in the center of Kandy is the Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Tooth) built by King Sri Rajasinghe in 1807 and still the heart of the Sinhalese Buddhist religion. It actually has more ancient origins (late 1600s early 1700s) and was always thought to guard the sacred tooth of the Buddha, one of his canine teeth, which remained after cremation and was brought to safety here from India.Since ancient times, the sacred tooth has been paraded through the streets of Kandy on the back of an elephant during the Esala Perahera a huge festival that attracts pilgrims from all over. Attending the Esala Perahera, which lasts 10 days between late July and August on dates that vary depending on the full moon, can be a unique experience.The temple itself does not possess the same attractions as other temples in Sri Lanka or other Buddhist countries but the devotion of pilgrims is tangible. The sanctuary is two-story and the interior has parts in exotic woods, lacquer and ivory. The tooth is upstairs.You must wear clothes that cover your legs and shoulders and remove your shoes.

body: Kandy, the enchanting hill capital of Sri Lanka, is renowned for its historical significance and natural splendour. This UNESCO World Heritage City, located 116 kilometres from Colombo, is celebrated for its lush landscapes and rich cultural heritage. At the heart of Kandy lies the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Dalada Maligawa), a sacred site revered by Buddhists around the globe. This temple, renowned for its beautiful Sinhalese architecture, houses the relic of Buddha’s tooth and continues to host ancient ceremonies with traditional drum performances daily.Kandy's cultural vibrancy is showcased in the Kandy Esala Perahera, an iconic annual festival held in July or August. This 10-day pageant is one of Sri Lanka’s grandest events, featuring a dazzling procession with over 100 richly adorned elephants, thousands of traditional dancers, drummers, and torch bearers. Originating from the 4th century, the Esala Perahera not only honors the sacred tooth relic but also brings together the community to celebrate Kandyan traditions and arts. The procession’s vibrant colors and rhythmic beats make it one of the most captivating cultural experiences in the world.

body: I am writing to express our deep concern and distress over an incident that occurred around 2pm, 27th of May 2024, which we believe contradicts the inclusive principles that Sri Dalada Maligawa, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, has long stood for.On the mentioned date, my wife was denied entry into the temple by the security personnel at the entry security scanning gate to Sri Dalada Maligawa. The reason provided was her attire – specifically, wearing of a “Hijab” (not Burkha as mentioned in website) which is similar to the head coverings of the Christian Nuns. This action was not only humiliating but also seemed to be in direct opposition to the Buddhist ideology of respect for all religions, which the temple is known to uphold.The exclusion based on religious attire is a matter of serious concern, as it directly impacts the fundamental rights of individuals to practice their religion and the values of respect and tolerance. It is imperative that the temple authorities address this issue promptly to ensure that the sacred space remains accessible and welcoming to all devotees, irrespective of their religious expressions.I’ve already requested in writing to the temple authorities to investigate this matter and take appropriate measures to prevent such incidents in the future maintaining respect the diverse backgrounds of visitors and to uphold the temple's commitment to religious harmony. Also, if “Hijab” which is similar to covering head like Nuns prohibited to entry then should mention clearly in websites publicly. So, it will save our time & effort to travel all the way there.

body: Sri Dalada Maligawa is our favorite place to visit in Kandy. It is a very important place for Sri Lankan Buddhists. Sri Dalada Maligawa, also known as the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, is a Buddhist temple in Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is considered the most sacred place of Buddhist worship in Sri Lanka and perhaps the world, housing the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. The temple is located in the Royal Palace Complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy. The relic has played an important role in Sri Lankan politics since ancient times, as it is believed that whoever holds the relic holds the governance of the country. The relic was historically held by Sinhalese kings. The temple of the tooth is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. A must-see if you are a tourist, this place is revered by Sri Lankan pilgrims.

body: When you hear the word “Buddha,” in the imagination of the ignorant, a statue of a man sitting in the “lotus” position immediately appears with a body proportional like a Nyagrodha tree, with membranes between the fingers, with an ushnisha on the top of the head, a smile with forty teeth, etc. In reality, this same Buddha is not just an idol sculpted from one material or another. Siddhartha Gautama Shakyamuni (aka Gautama Buddha) is a key figure in Buddhism: he is a spiritual teacher and the founder of Buddhism, one of the three world religions.Alas, as with all such personalities, there is little reliable information about the biography of the Buddha: a number of Buddhist sutras (texts) in Pali and several Sanskrit scriptures: “Buddacharita”, “Lalitavistara” and others. What is interesting is that when Buddha, at the age of 80, made the “Great Transition into the Absolute Peace of Nirvana,” his body was cremated in accordance with the rite for the Universal Ruler. But then all sorts of Epic Fails begin on the topic of “dividing the relics of the deceased.”If you believe the legends, the remains of the Buddha were divided into eight parts and lie at the base of specially erected stupas-suburgans - these are Buddhist architectural and sculptural religious structures of a hemispherical shape. So, when the relics of Buddha were being divided, someone cunning managed to steal the left fang of the deceased, which was taken to Ceylon. They say that Princess Hemamala and Prince Dantha from the city of Kalinga in India were involved in this action, and this happened during the reign of King Kirti Sri Meghavarna (sometime around 301-328 AD).In Ceylon, the TOOTH was declared a shrine and from that moment the history of the future Temple of the Sacred Relic of the Tooth Relic of Gautama Buddha, the Temple of the Tooth Relic, Sri Dalada Maligawa began!!! All these are names of the same religious building. And not just another Buddhist stupa, but one of the main and most revered shrines of the island!!! In Christianity, this question (I’m talking about sacred relics) is somehow more solid, or something: the Shroud of Turin, the Crown of Thorns, the Spear of Longinus, the Title INRI, the Holy Grail, nails (with which the body of Jesus was nailed to the Cross), and finally the pincers with which they took out those very nails... And then a TOOTH...A whole temple was built over it!!! The same existing Sri Dalada Maligawa in the city of Kandy, the capital of the Central Province of Sri Lanka. Like any shrine, from ancient times this TOOTH was attributed with a certain magical power - whoever owned the fang of the Buddha also had all the power. It is clear that under this “sauce” the Buddha tooth became the property of the ruling Sri Lankan royal dynasty. The fate of the TOOTH was turbulent: it was always kept in the temple at the royal residence, and since the capital “moved” several times (Anuradapura, Pollonnaruwa, Dambadeniya, Yapahuwa, Kurunegala, Kotte Gampola), the TOOTH “traveled” after it.Until he arrived in Kandy at the end of the 16th century. The first “Dalada Madura” (or “Dalada Mandira”, depending on how you write) to store the holy relic (I’m talking about the ZUB, of course) was built during the reign of King Vimaladharmasuriya I in 1592-1604. Alas, during the colonization of the island by the Portuguese, the temple was destroyed. The second sacral was erected on the same site during the reign of King Rajasinghe II from 1635 to 1687. Apparently, Temple of the Tooth was fatally unlucky - and this iconic building was burned, though now by the Dutch.In 1687, King Vimaladharmasuriya II built another Dalada Madura, and it had three floors!!! However, over time, the building fell into disrepair and was destroyed. And finally, his son, King Sri Vera Parakrama Narendrasinghe, who reigned from 1707 to 1739, built the current Dalada Maligawa, which, with minor architectural “adjustments” by subsequent rulers, has survived to this day. The architecture of the sacral is executed in a unique Kandyan style in combination with details and elements of the style of “Dalada Madura” - the forerunner sanctuaries, which previously housed the relic of the Sacred Tooth Relic of Buddha.The location chosen for the temple was simply magical: next to the ancient Royal Palace (the latter is located north of the temple) and a forest reserve called Udavatha Kelaya (to the east). The aura of this magnificent place is brightened by the famous Kandy Lake - the so-called Sea of Milk (also known as Bogambara and Kiri Mukhuda). I was probably lucky - there were practically no people (maybe it was just not the season), I refused the services of a guide - everything that interested me, I read on the internet the day before.I can’t say that I was deeply impressed by what I saw, but I recommend a visit to Sri Dalada Maligawa, if only because it is one of the most famous religious sites on the island.

body: This sacred site, nestled within the heart of the Kandy city, is a testament to the rich history and religious significance of Sri Lanka. The intricate carvings, vibrant paintings, and the imposing structure create an aura of grandeur, setting the stage for the profound experience that awaits inside. Main highlight of the temple is the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha enshrined within. The atmosphere inside the chamber is filled with a sense of reverence and devotion, as pilgrims and visitors alike gather to catch a glimpse of this revered relic. body: The Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, Sri Lanka, holds immense cultural and religious significance as it enshrines a tooth believed to be that of Buddha. Prayer time is 5.30am 6.30am 10.30am 6.30pm.Admission tickets, priced at approximately 2000 LKR, provide access to this UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Temple of the Tooth offers a profound spiritual experience amid its historical splendor.A highly recommended destination for those visiting Kandy, the Temple of the Tooth offers a profound and culturally enriching experience, deeply rooted in reverence and historical significance.

body: Kandy, a UNESCO World Heritage site, stands as the last capital of Sri Lanka's ancient kings. Nestled within its verdant hills is the revered Temple of the Tooth, which cradles the Buddha's sacred relic. This relic, symbolizing the living Buddha, has been a spiritual beacon for Buddhists for centuries. Historically, the tooth relic's possession signified governance, with kings seeking its blessings for prosperity and protection. The temple's grandeur reflects diverse architectural influences, from traditional Kandyan designs to intricate Indo-Aryan motifs. Each year, the temple's cultural vibrancy shines during the Esala Perahera, a grand procession drawing thousands with its displays of traditional arts and music.Many Buddhists globally journey to this sanctuary, immersing themselves in Sri Lanka's rich history, art, and traditions. The temple offers glimpses of traditional Kandyan performances, evoking a profound spiritual experience. Its architectural beauty, from the golden roof to delicate carvings, mesmerizes visitors. Beyond its tangible marvels, the Temple of the Tooth epitomizes values of peace, unity, and reverence, standing as a testament to Sri Lanka's historical legacy.To ensure a respectful visit, visitors are advised to observe Puja times at 5.45am 6:30am 10:30am and 6:30pm dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, preferably in white, and remove shoes upon entering."

Different prices for locals and for tourists are present also here, as everywhere else at Sri Lanka. The ceremony is a mass activity where a lot of people pushes themselves to a certain place at the temple, and you push yourself to get there also, since you don't know why are others pushing themselves so much. The fact it, the religious people want to give their offerings to the temple and to Buddha. You will end up in a room where everyone is packed, waiting to get to the room for offerings, where you won't get. So since you know about this now, you don't need to push yourself together with them and I have just saved you some time and nerves. Instead of pushing yourself with the mass, I recommend you to walk around the temple and the parts that are accessible for the visitors, and e.g. burn some candles as your offering outside. The place looks magical, especially in the evening when it's already dark outside. To burn something, you need to buy a special oil for that. I didn't figure out where to do that, unfortunately. What got me was a payment payment machine looking as an ATM that could be used for donations for the temple. Like wow. A way to go, The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic! This is what I call progress.

body: Considered as a sacred temple complex containing the sacred tooth relic of Lord Buddha, Shri Dalada Maligawa also known as Palace of sacred tooth.This temple is a must visit for every Buddhist.The tooth relic was originally housed in a rock carved temple in Anuradha pura before it was moved to the present palace / temple at Kandy about five hundred years ago.This centuries old temple is serene and the worshippers pray in silence.The temple was originally built as a royal residential palace by the royal family of Sri Lanka long time ago.The remarkable features of this temple is the renowned recital of Kandy drums is a joy to hear.The musical performance is unique for Sri Lanka.The musical instruments are two drums and a pipe instrument. The performance lasting about half an hour is precisely choreographed.The puja timings are fixed lasting about half an hour three times in a day - morning, noon and evening.The temple premises are very well secured and spotless maintenance is visible everywhere.You need to be properly dressed to enter the temple. Ensure that your shoulder and knees are covered.The temple management treats every body equal. No preference seems to be given for any one. There is no shouting at or pushing of the pilgrims in the sanctum sanctorium. Everything is done in dignified silence.The temple is a must visit while you are in Kandy, Sri Lanka.Highly recommended.

We hired a guide & got there around 5.45pm- just in time for us to enter the central premises & visit other shrines. Guide helped us navigate & explained the different parts of the temple in details. Some tips for fellow travellers- 1. The tooth relic is not for public viewing everyday- only taken our during ceremony. Instead we get to see the golden caskets holding the relic from 6.45pm in the evening. So get there on the right time! 2. Several shrines are present inside temple premises, like Crystal budhha, Hari Krishna, original manuscripts, museum & royal elephant memorial. Taking a guide is best to navigate & not miss out key sights. 3. Golden Canopy above the relic is not to be missed- stunning sight in the evening light! 4. Moonstone entrances, beautiful paintings & carvings- despite the rush, take sometime to admire the place.5. There are some ground rules for taking photographs- No selfies, no photos showing back to the Buddha statues, etc. So be mindful of them, while enjoying the temple. Entry fee for SAARC members is 1500 SLR per person. Ticket counter is next to the temple on side of the lake. Would suggest so spend atleast 1.5hrs to cover the entire temple.

body: We joined the queues during morning prayer. There are two queues to get in: one for the men and one for the women. Like most things in life, the men's line moved faster. This is mainly due to two things: 1) most women carry bags that need searching (most men don't) 2) the women perhaps face a little more scrutiny over what they can wear and must cover-up. Shoulders and legs need to be covered, so make sure you have a light scarf and sarong. Men too should carry a sarong to put on although some western males it seemed were managing to get through in shorts.Once inside make sure you follow the tourist crowds to the right and enter the temple through the tourist entry. Here you leave your shoes, you will be expected to tip after collection. Inside, at prayer, this place is busy. At times you are moved along with the crowd. The locals are of course queuing to leave gifts and to pray so don't feel too bad if you 'skip' queues and glide past those locals waiting on the stairs.The relic itself can't be seen. Instead, you can peer into the golden shrine where it is stored, but at this point in the temple, the crowds are at their busiest so you main only manage a cursory glance.The best part about the temple is exploring the grounds and additional rooms and buildings. The carvings and sculptures of Budha are beautiful, and in most spaces, you can take photos. Just be mindful of people worshipping and not to take pictures with your back to any Budha statue.The grounds of the temple are beautiful, and there is an elephant on the site too, which is used in ceremonies. Although, it is clearly an old elephant and seeing it so heavily chained doesn't make for the best view.At night time, around the temple and Lake, there is a cacophony of noise as bats and birds come to roost in their hundreds. It is the most spectacular site in Kandy and a must-see.The museum of World Buddhism, which is on the site is also worth a visit, and with a tourist ticket to the temple, you have access.

body: This is another UNESCO World Heritage Site with interesting history and background. The site is located in city centre of Kandy right in front of Kandy Lake. Tooth Relic is believed to be sacred for Buddhism and the royal family was responsible for the safekeeping of the tooth relic. It is believed to be brought from Anuradhapura to Kandy Kingdom. Two storeys building was constructed for safekeeping the tooth relic. But the building was destroyed several times. Each time it was restored whenever it was destroyed. There will be ceremony everyday for the blessings by the devotees. We visited around late afternoon and waited for the ceremony around 6pm plus. Interesting cultural sights, but be prepared for uncontrollable crowds and haphazard situation during the ceremony. The tooth relic is said to be kept within a gold plated ornament, hence it cannot be seen by anyone even during the ceremony. The international Buddhism Museum within the compound is worth to check out too for the interesting architecture and interior design. Overall, it is still worth the entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and appropriate attire is required and tight security check at the entrance.

body: We are a couple in early 30s with 9 and 10yr old daughters.Firstly we hadn't dressed appropriately so had to rent sarongs to cover up. We had a tip off from the sarong guy that they take away your cigarettes and lighters so I hid them well in the bag.You have to put your shoes in a shoe storage area. As atheists we were a little bemused by all of it. There's nothing to tell you where the tooth is. We assumed we were in the right place by the people praying on the floor... But there's no signs etc and we didn't have a guide.There's a museum which was a little interesting.The saddest part is the taxidermied elephant. Poor thing was captured and kept for a good 50years before he died. He's now stuffed in a glass cabinet. There's a photo timeline of his life since capture but it doesn't have any translation so we don't really know the story...If you like this sort if thing and are in Kandy then maybe pay it a visit... body: We were staying close to Kandy and knew that this was one of the biggest attractions in the area and our only available day to go was on a Saturday. We left early and got to the temple area around 9:30am. You must leave your shoes with a shoe keeper and buy your ticket in the same area. Make sure you are properly dressed as they will not let you in with any knee or shoulder showing (although you can buy a sarong right there if necessary). Women and men go through separate security lines and for us, the lines were extremely long and quite slow-I believe this was because of our timing. From there, you can make your way into the main temple and line up in a hectic, crowded, and sweaty manner for a VERY quick look at the golden casket which holds the sacred tooth of Buddha. From there, you are free to wander the grounds and look into the different buildings, including a museum with artifacts under glass, a room devoted to the famous temple elephant Raja the Tusker, and also some archeological artifacts. Altogether a very fascinating look into the passionate devotion to Buddha in Sri Lanka.

If you are lucky you may get a quick peek at the casket (with its separate 5 locks) where it is housed. If you are a tourist you can reach this by one very quick queue where Buddhists who wish to leave an offering may queue for 3 hours to reach the relic. The feeling of reference and respect is overwhelming and moving, just close your eyes for a moment and take in the sounds of chanting and drumming, the smells of essence and offerings, the emotions shown by people of faith. I can honestly say I felt completely overcome and still shiver at the memory.On leaving this area there is plenty more to see which are less crowded and easier to view. We particularly enjoyed the room with the pictures outlining the history of the sacred tooth around a statue of Buddha with another place for offeringsa must do place in Kandy, particularly if you can have an insight as to why it is so important to the people of Sri Lanka

body: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic is a Buddhist temple in the city of Kandy, Sri Lanka. It is located in the royal palace complex of the former Kingdom of Kandy. It is a very important Sri Lankan temple as it houses the relic of the tooth of the Buddha. We visited this temple as part of a G Adventures tour in the evening when the doors of the area where the casket that houses the tooth relic is open, This allows the locals as well as the tourists to see this casket. Due to problems with possible terrorists, there are high security measures taken before you can enter the temple. You must also be appropriately dressed with women wearing clothes that cover their shoulders and knees and men should wear full length pants. Most of the locals wear complete white outfits to show their respect when visiting the temple.It is a very busy in this temple and you cannot wear your shoes in it. I had a guide help me through the temple, which I would not have been able to do if he had not helped me up and down the numerous stairs you need to use to see the entire temple. The museum that is attached to the temple was also interesting to see as it held many sacred texts about Buddha's life.

body: The holy of holies for Sri Lankan Buddhists, the visit is a must though perhaps for tourists not at one of the scheduled pujas when you feel the crush of devotees attending to pray and offer food. If you want the atmosphere of a puja, drum beating will announce its start and continue throughout, the actual ceremony performed by the monks behind the closed temple doors with massive elephant tusks in front of it. The highlight is the ever so brief time you have looking at the large gold casket in the distance, devotees handing food and flowers over to the monks. Visit the library with its Buddhist texts on palm leaf and dazzle at some of the jewel-encrusted vases and the like. In another area you can get a history of the tooth relic over 21 panels. As you exit, the grounds are rather pretty. While there are elements of the visit that will leave you dissatisfied, try to soak up the overall atmosphere. You have to go through security.

body: Religious site with a Buddha tooth relic with a newer building built over the original relic casket. Been told that at twice a day the casket door will be opened for special prayers. The tooth relic was brought over by the King and Queen, and she hid the relic in her hair, when the capital was moved to Kandy. Every year in August, the Festival of the Tooth is one of the grandest festivals in Sri Lanka and in the Buddhist world. It is held every summer in Kandy to honor the sacred tooth of Lord Buddha and to pay homage to old gods of Sri Lanka. For the people of Sri Lanka, it is a time to celebrate the country's rich culture and history

body: Get your information and timing right if you wish to visit this ancient and holy place. The door to the main relic is opened at specific timings, so check before you plan your trip. While the doors to the main shrine are closed, the crowds start building up, so if crowds scare you this place is an absolute no. Although the crowds are quite well behaved. Be sure to cover your shoulders and legs else shell out money to locals for giving you wraps etc. You need to buy tickets at the entrance from kiosks which need exact change. You will need to remove and deposit shoes at the counters outside. Once inside it gives you the feel of an ancient place but well preserved and maintained. Lots of devotees with offerings throng the temple every day. Do not miss the oil lamps lighted outside by numerous devotees. You are allowed to take pictures but take care not to have your back towards the main shrine - else you will be asked to delete them by the vigilant guards. You marvel at the architecture of the temple and palace and leaves you asking fir more. The gardens are huge and well kept. I would recommend going there in the evenings, and once the temple visit is done you can enjoy the beauty of the kandy lake and the hills in the background.

body: The number one tourist destination in Kandy is surely this Temple. Easy to find in central Kandy. The entrance is adjacent to the old Victoria Hotel. Be aware that your legs and shoulders must be covered (no shorts allowed), so local sellers do sell some wraps or baggy loose trousers for a fee. Once in, a short stroll through the garden to the museum itself. If you are not native to Sri Lanka, you must go to the right to deposit your shoes in a locker/storage area before then queuing, searching and enter the temple. You also may want to pick up lotus or incense offerings before you go in too. Follow the crowds, it’s easy to navigate, and try not to take too many photos inside (which may offend) and pay the appropriate respects to those there for religious purposes. There is also a museum on site too towards the rear of the temple that’s worth a look too.

body: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth holds Sri Lanka's most sacred Relic, a tooth of the Buddha. Unfortunately we did not get to see the casket housing the Relic, but were still awed by the beauty of the architecture and the décor of the frescoes, moonstones and wooden frames. See the beautiful seated statue of a golden Buddha flanked by two white marble statues, other images and the ivory tusks, and then look to the ornamentation of the ceiling above. The Main Hall showcases man statue of the Buddha in various poses; suspended plaques over each give an explanation of he painted scene above. At ceiling height, above each statue, there is a sculpture of an elephant head and tusks, all coloured gold. Some wonderful features both indoors and to the buildings' exteriors. The complex was crowed with tourists and worshippers, sound muted as if all acknowledge the sanctity of the place.

body: I spent half the day at this by far the most relevant sightseeing spot at Kelly. I recommend to visit late in the afternoon if you get the chance to see the ceremony at 18:30. I managed with a beach towel which made some locals laugh but it did its job 😉.The interior is awesome but I would also advice to reserve some time to wander around the surrounds. Around 4-5pm it tends to rain like the end of the world quite often.
place_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
title: A must do in Kandy

body: A must visit place to understand the Buddhist inroads into Sri Lanka from India...A serene place with beautiful surrounding ambiance. Actually a royal palace converted to Temple to house the Tooth Relic....The 2 floor museum is also interesting.
place_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
title: Serene & Sacred

body: This is a nice temple to visit.However, they are the most restrict temple that I visited during our visit in Sri Lanka in regards to dress code. They refused to let me in with scarfs wrapped around my skirt since they were see through. I had to finally rent appropriate thick material skirt to put on as the skirt I was originally was wearing was slightly above my knees.Guys must have long pants or wrapped in cloth to cover below knees.They charge 1500 Rupees for forigner to enter the temple.
place_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
title: Nice to visit

body: I really enjoyed visiting this temple. Bare in mind they are very strict with dressing. The shoulders must be covers and the dress must be under knees and not see through otherwise they will not let you in.The ticket cost around 8$. You can not see the Tooth relic and it's sealed in 7 coffins and they rarely take it out. You will leave your shoes at the entrance so if you go in the afternoon the pavement might be hot.
place_name: Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic
title: Sacred Temple

body: This is the famous Buddhist temple which has the tooth relic of Buddha. The annual festival of perehera . The tooth relic is taken around town in an elephant once a year.

title: Buddhist

body: It is great temple and maintained very well. I enjoyed the time at this temple. It is maintained very well and has good Security measures in place.

title: Great place to visit

body: Some tips. Entrance ticket price for a foreigner is Rs1500. Better to carry the exact amount. Dress - Make sure you cover your shoulders, pant should be below knees and shouldn't be tight, colour doesn't matter. If it's a sunny time, better to wear socks since you have to enter without shoes.

title: Amazing!

body: All te staff were very friendly and there will be a guide once you have put your shoes into the shoe bar. The guide was fantastic and as I was a solo traveller he was happy to take the photos of me at the right placed.

title: Beautiful place to visit.

body: I went to the temple at night and it was still very busy. My experience was of feeling very spiritual. The ceiling frescos and buildings are amazing. When in Kandy this is a must.

title: Spiritual and Humbling

body: After reading some poor reviews nd being told the entrance cost 4000 Sri lankan rupies, we decided to take a trip there just to walk around the lake. However, after being informed by a tour guide that it actually costs 1500 we decided to go ahead. Although it was busy with people worshiping, as it was a special holy day,it was not Iver crowded and we were able to see and hear everything the tour guide showed us. I found the information quite interesting however the best bit was getting a real insight into Buddhist worship. The your guide expected 1000 tip each, which he made quite clear from the start

body: We were lucky to stay for the evening viewing of the tooth casket. Overall the temple is as gorgeous as any of the Buddhist temples in the world.But the Buddhist museum behind the temple which is easily accessible with the same entry tickets was beautiful & educative for the kids too.

body: 1 the ticket is 1500 R, about 8.3 USD per person. 2 remember to cover your shoulders and knees. 3 be ready to walk around with bare feet from entrance onwards. 4 the relic only shows to the public every 10 years. When we visited, we heard the last time the relic was out of the container eight years ago. Every day 6:30 pm, people cn line up to see the container with the relic.

title: Worth a visit but you wont see the relic

body: We visited the temple early in the day when it wasn’t too busy but be prepared for a reasonable sized crowd. There is plenty to see including the museum sections which are worth the time. Try and be around for the offering time. We saw one at 9.30 am. It happens three times a day - it is also the busiest time. Enjoy this wonderful place.
